extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishers (including self-published authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the parts of a book (copyright page, front matter, text divisions, back matter), including what to include, placement, formatting, and conventions for editions, printings, and metadata. Intended to govern production and editorial decisions for printed and electronic books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include ISBN for each format
rubrics_metrics.description: An International Standard Book Number (ISBN) should appear and uniquely identify the book; each format or binding must have a separate ISBN (hardcover, paperbound, e-book, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ISBN should appear on the copyright page and on the jacket or cover. If practical, list all ISBNs on the copyright page when formats are published simultaneously. Agencies (Bowker, International ISBN Agency) provide assignment and resources for publishers and self-published authors. Some monograph-series books may also receive an ISSN.

rubrics_metrics.name: List a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) if available
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers registered with DOI agencies (e.g., Crossref) should list the DOI that refers to the book as a whole on the copyright page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crossref recommends presenting the DOI as a link (https://doi.org/...). Like the ISBN, the DOI should appear on the jacket or cover and be included in the book's metadata. Always present the DOI as a link when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: For translations, indicate original-language title, publisher, and copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book is a translation, record the original title, publisher, and copyright information on the copyright page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information is typically required by contract with the original publisher and is illustrated in the manual (fig. 1.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include acknowledgments, permissions, and other credits where space permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright page may include acknowledgments of previously published parts, illustration credits, and permissions to quote copyrighted material, unless such acknowledgments appear elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If space is limited, place longer acknowledgments in a separate front- or back-matter acknowledgments section. Some publishers credit designers on the copyright page. See chapter 4 for full permissions discussion and 3.29-37 for illustration credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Cataloging-in-Publication (CIP) data when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: US publishers commonly print Library of Congress CIP data on copyright pages for books made available to libraries; CIP may also cover simultaneously published e-book versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply for CIP, consult the Library of Congress online resources. Publishers not participating may use the Preassigned Control Number (PCN) program. Only US publishers are eligible for CIP/PCN; other countries (Canada, UK/Ireland, Australia) have similar programs and different self-publishing eligibility rules. Self-publishers in the US are generally not eligible for CIP but may be for PCN.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a paper durability statement if standards are met
rubrics_metrics.description: Books meeting ANSI/NISO (and ISO) permanence standards may carry a notice that the paper meets permanence requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the prescribed wording (e.g., 'This paper meets the requirements of ANSI/NISO Z39.48-1992 (Permanence of Paper).') and the permanent paper sign (circled infinity) where applicable. Publishers may also include logos/statements for recycled or sustainably sourced paper per relevant certifying organizations. Such statements may be omitted in electronic formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide publisher's address (and contact info for self-published authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher's address (and sometimes overseas agents) is typically listed on the copyright page; the publisher's homepage URL may also appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses may be abbreviated (city and postal code). Self-published authors may include contact information to facilitate reader correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright notice composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual copyright notice consists of the symbol ©, the first year the book is published, and the name of the copyright owner; may be followed by 'All rights reserved' and publication date or publishing history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The year of publication should correspond to the copyright date; prefer the later date if the book is physically available at year-end but formally published in the next year. Publishers often copyright in the organization's name, though authors may copyright in their own names; see fuller discussion elsewhere (4.39-46).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include copyright dates of previous editions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Each substantially new edition gets a new copyright date; include the copyright dates of at least the most recent previous editions in the copyright notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the new edition is so extensive that it virtually constitutes a new publication, previous copyright dates may be omitted. Distinguish editions from impressions and paperback/electronic versions that do not constitute new editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show copyright renewal or changes in ownership when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a copyright has been renewed or assigned, the renewal or change may be reflected in the notice (e.g., '© 1963 by X. © renewed 1991 by X.'), and the new owner's name substituted when ownership changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copyright date remains unless renewed. Copyrights remain legally valid even if renewal or reassignment information cannot appear in a new edition or printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing history content and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing history usually follows the copyright notice and begins with the year of original publication, followed by number/date of editions; for long histories, listing original and latest edition is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previous publisher's name need not be given unless required by licensing. Items may appear on separate lines or the same line separated by periods. Examples: 'First edition published 1906. Seventeenth edition 2017.' or 'Revised edition originally published 1999. University of Chicago Press edition 2010.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Define what constitutes a new edition
rubrics_metrics.description: A new edition is one in which a substantial change has been made in essential elements of the work; as a general rule, at least 20 percent of a new edition should consist of new or revised material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work republished with only a new preface or typographical corrections is better described as a new impression or reissue. 'Edition' may also label a reissue in a different format or imprint. Edition designation (Second Edition, Third Edition) appears on the title page; terms like 'revised and expanded' are optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record country of printing
rubrics_metrics.description: The country in which a book is printed is usually identified on the copyright page; if printed in a country different from publication, the jacket or cover must state this (e.g., 'Printed in China').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country-of-printing information may be omitted for electronic formats but need not be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impression numbering and versioning practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers' impression lines may indicate impressions/printings (a series of digits used by some publishers) or explicit statements (e.g., 'Second printing, May 2020'); impression lines help track corrections made between printings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital print-on-demand and e-book publishing require different versioning: e-books can use ISBN/DOI plus a last-modified date (EPUB standard) or software-like version numbers (1.0, 1.0.1, 1.1, 2.0). Such version information belongs in metadata and may appear on the copyright page or elsewhere per publisher policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record original-language edition information on translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Original-language title, publisher, and copyright of the source edition should be recorded on the copyright page of the translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This typically fulfills contractual obligations with original publishers and provides bibliographic clarity (see fig. 1.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge grants and subsidies properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should acknowledge grants of financial assistance toward publication on the copyright page when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wording, placement, and logo use should follow grantor specifications or approval. Financial assistance to authors is usually noted in the author's acknowledgments section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place acknowledgments and permissions appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgments requiring more space or prominence may appear in a separate section in front or back matter; acknowledgments of previously published parts and permissions can be placed on the copyright page if space permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If acknowledgments appear elsewhere (preface, acknowledgments section, source notes), they need not be duplicated on the copyright page. For illustration credits see 3.29-37 and permissions see chapter 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of contents placement and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The table of contents for a printed work usually begins on page vi or vii (depending on dedication/epigraph placement) and should include all preliminary material that follows it but exclude anything that precedes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List title and beginning page number of each section: front matter, text divisions, and back matter including index. If book is divided into parts, part titles appear but their page numbers are omitted unless parts include separate introductions. Subheads within chapters are usually omitted unless they provide valuable signposts. In multiauthor volumes list each chapter author in the contents.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of illustrations/tables: when and how to include
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of illustrations or tables is not essential if the book has very few or many illustrations tightly tied to the text; in appropriate cases include a list matching the table of contents in type size/style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide lists into Figures, Tables, Plates, Drawings, Maps as needed. Page numbers are given for illustrations printed with the text and counted in pagination; for galleries printed on different stock and not counted, indicate 'Facing page 000' or 'Following page 000' in the list or table of contents. Titles in lists may be shortened or adjusted (see 8.157-67).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontispiece naming and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A frontispiece is not assigned a page number; its location is simply given as 'frontispiece'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of its prominent front position, indicate location rather than pagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreword usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve 'Foreword' for prefatory remarks by someone other than the author (including an editor), especially if the work already has an author's preface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foreword is set in the same size/style as the text, normally runs a few pages, and the author's name usually appears at the end. The publisher may note the foreword on the title page (e.g., 'With a Foreword by...'). If a foreword is substantial it may bear the author's name at the beginning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface and acknowledgments conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's statement about a work is usually called a preface and includes reasons for undertaking the work, research method (if relevant), brief acknowledgments, and sometimes permissions; set in same size/style as text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preface need not be signed, but if signed the signature appears at the end. New prefaces for new editions should precede the original preface, which may be retitled (e.g., 'Preface to the First Edition'). In books with both an editor's and an author's preface, the editor's preface comes first and should bear the editor's name at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate acknowledgments placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Long acknowledgments may be put in a separate section following the preface or at the back of the book; acknowledgments applying to all volumes of a multivolume work may be presented only in the first volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a preface consists only of acknowledgments, the title should be changed to 'Acknowledgments'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between front-matter and text introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: An introduction that is part of front matter should discuss the book as a whole (origins, acknowledgments) rather than the subject matter; most introductions belong in the main text and carry arabic page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A substantial introduction by someone other than the author is usually front matter and may be called a foreword if 3–5 pages or less. A text introduction integral to subject matter should not include acknowledgments and is paginated with the main text.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of abbreviations usage and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a list of abbreviations when many abbreviations are used or a few are used frequently; its location should be given in the table of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If abbreviations are used in text or footnotes, place the list in front matter; if used only in back matter, place list before the first element where they appear. Alphabetize by abbreviation, not spelled-out form. Do not use the list as a substitute for spelling out terms at first occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher's, translator's, and editor's notes placement and typographic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on the text are usually treated typographically like a preface or foreword and placed accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A publisher's note (rare) should precede or immediately follow the table of contents. A translator's note should precede any element by the original author. Editor's methodological notes for scholarly editions may appear in front or back matter; brief editorial method remarks are often better placed in an editor's preface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining page 1
rubrics_metrics.description: The first page of the first chapter or the main-text introduction is usually counted as arabic page 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When front matter is extensive, include a second half title before the text that is counted as page 1 (though the number does not appear); the following verso is usually blank or may contain an illustration or epigraph. A part-title page can similarly be treated as page 1 when a book begins with a part title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-introduction conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A text introduction integral to the subject matter should not include acknowledgments or other front/back matter material; it carries arabic page numbers and is usually shorter than a chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable for a text introduction to outline chapter contents, but authors may prefer to limit such content to a preface. Consider adding a descriptive subtitle even to shorter introductions; avoid titling chapter 1 simply 'Introduction' without a more evocative title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into parts: structure and minimum content
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts carry a number and title and should contain at least two chapters (except for parts that include only an introductory or concluding chapter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters are numbered consecutively throughout the book (do not restart numbering in each part). Part titles that do not include introductions usually begin recto with a blank verso; part introductions may begin on recto, the verso, or the part title itself. No part title is needed before back matter, though one may be useful before appendixes or notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into chapters: titles, openings, and displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Most nonfiction prose works are divided into numbered chapters of consistent length; chapter titles should be short and descriptive and each chapter normally starts on a new page with a chapter display (number, title, subtitle if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter opening page should carry a drop folio (or sometimes no folio) and no running head. Note reference numbers/symbols traditionally do not appear in the chapter display; an unnumbered note referring to a chapter as a whole may precede numbered notes. Chapter epigraphs may be considered part of the chapter display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter authorship conventions for multiauthor books
rubrics_metrics.description: In multiauthor books, the chapter author's name is usually given at the head of each chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affiliation or identifying information may be placed in an unnumbered footnote on the chapter's first page or in a list of contributors. An unnumbered footnote can disclose source information for reprinted chapters. For e-book formats lacking footnote support, source or author notes may need to appear immediately after the chapter title or be linked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisions for poetry: unpublished vs previously published
rubrics_metrics.description: In a book of previously unpublished poetry, each poem usually begins on a new page; in a collection of previously published poems, multiple poems may appear on the same page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part titles provided by the poet should appear on separate pages (rectos) preceding grouped poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisions for letters and diaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and diaries are usually presented in chronological order and are seldom divided into chapters or parts; headings (dates, sender/recipient names) serve as section markers and typically do not begin new pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dates in headings when not present in the letter itself; correspondence headings generally do not start new pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion placement and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The main text may end with a conclusion that summarizes or poses further questions; a conclusion may take the form of a final chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conclusion may begin recto or verso, but in books divided into parts it should begin recto to avoid appearing to belong only to the final part. Consider giving a concluding chapter a descriptive title rather than 'Conclusion'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epilogue/afterword conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An epilogue or afterword is a relatively brief section commenting on the text or bringing the narrative up to date; when added to a new edition or written by a different author it is often called an afterword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epilogue/afterword generally follows any conclusion and may begin recto or verso, but should usually begin recto in books with parts or when appended to a new edition. It is set in the same size and style as the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subhead wording and first-sentence rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Subheads within chapters should be short, meaningful, and parallel in structure and tone; the first sentence following a subhead should not refer syntactically to the subhead (words may be repeated where necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: use 'The secondary spongiosa, a vaulted structure...' rather than 'This vaulted structure...' after the subhead 'SECONDARY SPONGIOSA.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Subhead levels and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Many works require only one subhead level; technical works may require more (A-level, B-level, C-level). Only the most complicated works need more than three levels; a lower-level subhead may follow an upper-level one with no intervening text but ideally subdivisions should have at least two subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate levels by type style and placement. The lowest level can be a run-in subhead (set in italics or bold and followed by a period), usually capitalized sentence-style. The number of subhead levels may vary chapter to chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbered subheads: when to use multilevel numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless sections are cited elsewhere, numbers are usually unnecessary for subheads; in scientific/technical works numbering provides easy reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple numeration (chapter.section.subsection) is the common system (e.g., 4.12.3). This manual uses chapter number followed by paragraph number for cross-referencing. Numbering can also be applied to illustrations, tables, and equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamental or typographic breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a break stronger than a paragraph but weaker than a subhead is required, use asterisks, type ornaments, or a blank line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blank lines can be missed at page bottoms or in electronic reflowable text; to avoid misses, differentiate the first few words of the paragraph following the break (e.g., with small capitals). Whatever strategy is used, maintain it consistently across publication formats.
